subject: Claude CCAF: Tool Design & MCP Integration
chapter: 2.8 Tool Interface Design, Descriptions & Response Shaping
description: NEW TOPIC. Writing tool descriptions that drive reliable selection, input_examples for complex inputs, consolidating operations, namespacing, shaping tool responses for high signal, and the constraints on forced tool use. Grounded in the official Claude API define-tools documentation.

questions.question: What does the documentation call by far the most important factor in tool performance?
options: Extremely detailed descriptions covering what the tool does, when it should and shouldn't be used, what each parameter means, and any caveats or limitations.
A tightly constrained input_schema with every field required.
A short, memorable tool name.
Setting strict: true on every tool.
questions.answer: Extremely detailed descriptions covering what the tool does, when it should and shouldn't be used, what each parameter means, and any caveats or limitations.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: best practices
questions.explanation:
'Provide extremely detailed descriptions. This is by far the most important factor in tool performance.' The listed contents: what the tool does, when it should be used (and when it shouldn't), what each parameter means and how it affects behaviour, and 'Any important caveats or limitations, such as what information the tool does not return if the tool name is unclear.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Over-constraining forces guessed values, the same failure as an all-required extraction schema.
- **C.** Names matter for disambiguation but carry far less information than descriptions.
- **D.** strict guarantees argument conformance, not correct selection.

The stated target length: 'Aim for at least 3-4 sentences for each tool description, more if the tool is complex.'
questions.examTrick: 3-4 sentences MINIMUM per description, including when NOT to use it and what it does not return.

questions.question: A team has separate tools named create_pr, review_pr, and merge_pr. What does the documentation recommend?
options: Consolidate related operations into a single tool with an action parameter — fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity.
Keep them separate so each description can be maximally specific.
Merge them into one tool with no parameters and let Claude infer the operation from context.
Split them further, one tool per PR field.
questions.answer: Consolidate related operations into a single tool with an action parameter — fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: best practices
questions.explanation:
'Consolidate related operations into fewer tools. Rather than creating a separate tool for every action (create_pr, review_pr, merge_pr), group them into a single tool with an action parameter. Fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity and make your tool surface easier for Claude to navigate.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** More tools means more near-neighbours to disambiguate, and every definition costs tokens on every request.
- **C.** Removing the parameter removes the model's ability to state its intent explicitly.
- **D.** The opposite direction entirely.

Note the tension with the previous item: descriptions should be long, and tool COUNT should be low. Both push the same way — invest depth in fewer, well-described tools.
questions.examTrick: Consolidate with an action parameter. Fewer, richer tools beat many thin ones for both selection and token cost.

questions.question: Why does the documentation recommend namespacing tool names such as github_list_prs and slack_send_message?
options: It makes tool selection unambiguous as the library grows, and is especially important when using tool search.
It is required by the tool name regex.
It reduces the token cost of the tool definition.
It groups tools so only one namespace loads at a time.
questions.answer: It makes tool selection unambiguous as the library grows, and is especially important when using tool search.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: best practices
questions.explanation:
'Use meaningful namespacing in tool names. When your tools span multiple services or resources, prefix names with the service (for example, github_list_prs, slack_send_message). This makes tool selection unambiguous as your library grows, and is especially important when using tool search.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** The regex is ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$ — underscores are allowed but namespacing is not required by it.
- **C.** Longer names cost marginally more, not less.
- **D.** Namespacing is a naming convention, not a loading mechanism.

This mirrors MCP's own convention, where tools are addressed as mcp__<server>__<tool> — the server segment is the namespace.
questions.examTrick: Namespace by service. Name regex is ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$. Matters most under tool search.

questions.question: How should a tool's RESPONSE be designed?
options: Return only high-signal information: semantic, stable identifiers such as slugs or UUIDs rather than opaque internal references, and only the fields Claude needs for its next step.
Return the full upstream API payload so nothing is lost.
Return a natural-language summary rather than structured data.
Return internal database row IDs so the agent can join records efficiently.
questions.answer: Return only high-signal information: semantic, stable identifiers such as slugs or UUIDs rather than opaque internal references, and only the fields Claude needs for its next step.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: best practices
questions.explanation:
'Design tool responses to return only high-signal information. Return semantic, stable identifiers (for example, slugs or UUIDs) rather than opaque internal references, and include only the fields Claude needs to reason about its next step. Bloated responses waste context and make it harder for Claude to extract what matters.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Full payloads are the documented anti-pattern — they waste context and bury the signal.
- **C.** Structure is useful; the guidance is about VOLUME and identifier quality, not format.
- **D.** Opaque internal references are exactly what the guidance says to avoid, because they carry no meaning the model can reason with.

The cost angle: tool_result blocks are input tokens on every subsequent request in the loop, so a bloated response is paid for repeatedly, not once.
questions.examTrick: High-signal responses with SEMANTIC identifiers. Bloated tool results are re-paid on every later turn of the loop.

questions.question: What is the input_examples field for, and what are its limitations?
options: An optional array of schema-valid example inputs for complex tools; each must validate against input_schema or you get a 400, it is unsupported on server tools and the computer-use and browser-use toolsets, and examples add roughly 20-50 tokens each (100-200 for complex nested objects).
A list of example outputs the tool may return.
A required field for any tool with more than one parameter.
A free-form prose section describing typical usage.
questions.answer: An optional array of schema-valid example inputs for complex tools; each must validate against input_schema or you get a 400, it is unsupported on server tools and the computer-use and browser-use toolsets, and examples add roughly 20-50 tokens each (100-200 for complex nested objects).
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: providing tool use examples
questions.explanation:
'Add an optional input_examples field to your tool definition with an array of example input objects. Each example must be valid according to the tool's input_schema.' The requirements and limitations: schema validation with 'Invalid examples return a 400 error'; not supported for server-side tools or the computer use and browser use client toolsets; and token cost of '~20-50 tokens for simple examples, ~100-200 tokens for complex nested objects'. It is 'particularly useful for complex tools with nested objects, optional parameters, or format-sensitive inputs.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** They are INPUT examples.
- **C.** Optional, and the docs say to 'Prioritize descriptions' first.
- **D.** They are structured objects, not prose.

The documented example deliberately includes one entry that omits the optional unit field — demonstrating to the model that omission is legitimate.
questions.examTrick: input_examples are schema-validated (400 if not), cost 20-200 tokens each, and can demonstrate that an optional field may be OMITTED.

questions.question: Which description is closer to the documented 'good' example?
options: 'Retrieves the current stock price for a given ticker symbol. The ticker must be valid for a publicly traded company on a major US exchange like NYSE or NASDAQ. Returns the latest trade price in USD. Use when the user asks about the current or most recent price of a specific stock. It will not provide any other information about the stock or company.'
'Gets the stock price for a ticker.'
'Stock price tool.'
'Returns financial data.'
questions.answer: 'Retrieves the current stock price for a given ticker symbol. The ticker must be valid for a publicly traded company on a major US exchange like NYSE or NASDAQ. Returns the latest trade price in USD. Use when the user asks about the current or most recent price of a specific stock. It will not provide any other information about the stock or company.'
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: good vs poor description
questions.explanation:
This is the documented good example. The docs analyse it: 'The good description clearly explains what the tool does, when to use it, what data it returns, and what the ticker parameter means. The poor description is too brief and leaves Claude with many open questions about the tool's behavior and usage.' Option B is the documented POOR example verbatim.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** All are too brief to guide selection or argument construction.

Notice the four jobs the good description does: capability, constraints on valid input, what comes back and in what unit, and an explicit negative boundary ('will not provide any other information'). That last clause is what stops the model reaching for this tool when asked about market cap.
questions.examTrick: A good description does four jobs: what it does, valid input constraints, what it returns (with units), and what it does NOT do.

questions.question: Which model guidance does the documentation give for tool complexity?
options: Use Claude Opus 5 for complex tools and ambiguous queries since it handles multiple tools better and seeks clarification; use Haiku models for straightforward tools, noting they may infer missing parameters.
Use Haiku for complex tools since speed matters more with many tools.
Model choice does not affect tool-use quality.
Always use Opus regardless of tool complexity.
questions.answer: Use Claude Opus 5 for complex tools and ambiguous queries since it handles multiple tools better and seeks clarification; use Haiku models for straightforward tools, noting they may infer missing parameters.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: choosing a model
questions.explanation:
'Use the latest Claude Opus model, Claude Opus 5, for complex tools and ambiguous queries; it handles multiple tools better and seeks clarification when needed. Use Claude Haiku models for straightforward tools, but note they may infer missing parameters.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Reversed.
- **C.** The docs are explicit that behaviour differs, particularly around missing required parameters.
- **D.** Haiku is recommended for straightforward tools, and cost matters.

The 'may infer missing parameters' warning is the design consequence: on a smaller model, an under-specified request produces a guessed argument rather than a clarifying question. Design your schemas and validation for that.
questions.examTrick: Opus for complex/ambiguous (asks for clarification). Haiku for simple tools (may GUESS missing parameters).

questions.question: What does the API do internally when you pass the tools parameter?
options: It constructs a special system prompt from the tool definitions, tool configuration, and any user-specified system prompt, instructing the model how to use the tools.
It validates each tool by calling it once with sample input.
It converts the tools into a fine-tuned adapter for the request.
It appends the tool definitions to the last user message.
questions.answer: It constructs a special system prompt from the tool definitions, tool configuration, and any user-specified system prompt, instructing the model how to use the tools.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: tool use system prompt
questions.explanation:
'When you call the Claude API with the tools parameter, the API constructs a special system prompt from the tool definitions, tool configuration, and any user-specified system prompt.' The documented skeleton includes formatting instructions, the tool definitions in JSON Schema, your system prompt, and the tool configuration.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** No test invocation occurs.
- **C.** No adaptation happens.
- **D.** It is a system prompt, not a user-message append.

This explains the token table from the pricing section: the tool-use system prompt is why tool_choice values cost different amounts, and why 'If no tools are provided, then a tool choice of none uses 0 additional system prompt tokens.'
questions.examTrick: Tools become a constructed SYSTEM PROMPT. That is why tool_choice changes the token count.

questions.question: What is a documented side effect of setting tool_choice to any or tool?
options: The API prefills the assistant message to force a tool call, so the model emits no natural-language response or explanation before the tool_use blocks, even if explicitly asked to.
The model always calls every provided tool in parallel.
The tool's input_schema is ignored.
The response is returned as plain text rather than content blocks.
questions.answer: The API prefills the assistant message to force a tool call, so the model emits no natural-language response or explanation before the tool_use blocks, even if explicitly asked to.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: forcing tool use
questions.explanation:
'Note that when you have tool_choice as any or tool, the API prefills the assistant message to force a tool to be used. This means that the models will not emit a natural language response or explanation before tool_use content blocks, even if explicitly asked to do so.' The documented workaround: 'If you would like the model to provide natural language context or explanations while still requesting that the model use a specific tool, you can use {"type": "auto"} for tool_choice (the default) and add explicit instructions in a user message. For example: What's the weather like in London? Use the get_weather tool in your response.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None is documented.

The docs add reassurance on quality: 'Testing has shown that this should not reduce performance.'
questions.examTrick: Forcing (any/tool) suppresses the model's explanatory text. Want both? Use auto + an explicit instruction in the user message.

questions.question: Which tool_choice values are incompatible with MANUAL extended thinking?
options: any and tool — only auto and none are compatible with manual extended thinking, though adaptive thinking supports forced tool use.
auto and none — forcing is required when thinking is enabled.
All four are incompatible with any form of thinking.
There is no interaction between thinking and tool_choice.
questions.answer: any and tool — only auto and none are compatible with manual extended thinking, though adaptive thinking supports forced tool use.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: forcing tool use
questions.explanation:
'When using manual extended thinking (thinking: {type: "enabled"}) with tool use, tool_choice: {"type": "any"} and tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "..."} are not supported and result in an error. Only tool_choice: {"type": "auto"} (the default) and tool_choice: {"type": "none"} are compatible with manual extended thinking. Adaptive thinking, including on models where thinking is on by default such as Claude Opus 5, supports forced tool use.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Reversed.
- **C.** Adaptive thinking supports forcing.
- **D.** There is a documented interaction that produces an error.

A second constraint in the same area: 'Claude Mythos Preview does not support forced tool use. Requests with tool_choice any or tool return a 400 error on this model.'
questions.examTrick: Manual extended thinking + forced tool use = error. Adaptive thinking is fine. Mythos Preview never supports forcing.

questions.question: How does changing tool_choice interact with prompt caching?
options: It invalidates cached message blocks; tool definitions and system prompts remain cached, but message content must be reprocessed.
It invalidates the entire cache including tool definitions.
It has no effect on caching.
It extends the cache TTL to one hour automatically.
questions.answer: It invalidates cached message blocks; tool definitions and system prompts remain cached, but message content must be reprocessed.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: forcing tool use note
questions.explanation:
'When using prompt caching, changes to the tool_choice parameter will invalidate cached message blocks. Tool definitions and system prompts remain cached, but message content must be reprocessed.' This matches the caching invalidation table, where 'Tool choice → invalidates messages cache only'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** That is what changing tool DEFINITIONS does — invalidating tools, system, and messages.
- **C.** There is a documented effect.
- **D.** TTL is set by cache_control, not by tool_choice.

The design implication: switching tool_choice per request in an agentic loop has a real, repeated cost. If you need forcing only sometimes, consider whether prompting under auto would do.
questions.examTrick: tool_choice change = messages cache only. tool DEFINITIONS change = all three levels. Know the blast radii.

questions.question: Which combination guarantees both that a tool is called and that its inputs match the schema?
options: tool_choice: {"type": "any"} combined with strict: true on the tool definitions.
strict: true alone.
tool_choice: {"type": "any"} alone.
input_examples plus a detailed description.
questions.answer: tool_choice: {"type": "any"} combined with strict: true on the tool definitions.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: guaranteed tool calls with strict tools
questions.explanation:
'Combine tool_choice: {"type": "any"} with strict tool use to guarantee both that one of your tools will be called AND that the tool inputs strictly follow your schema. Set strict: true on your tool definitions to enable schema validation.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** strict validates a call that happens; it cannot force one.
- **C.** Forcing produces a call whose arguments are not guaranteed to conform.
- **D.** Examples and descriptions improve reliability probabilistically; neither is a guarantee.

This is the two-orthogonal-guarantees idea stated by the docs themselves, and it is the answer to any exam scenario where a conversational reply or a malformed argument would break a downstream system.
questions.examTrick: any + strict = both guarantees. Neither alone is sufficient for a downstream system that cannot tolerate either failure.

questions.question: Claude often emits explanatory text before calling a tool under tool_choice auto. How should your code treat that?
options: Treat it like any other assistant-generated text and do not rely on specific formatting conventions, since Claude may use various phrasings.
Parse it for a structured intent marker that always precedes tool calls.
Discard the whole response as malformed.
Assume it is always absent and index content[0] as the tool_use block.
questions.answer: Treat it like any other assistant-generated text and do not rely on specific formatting conventions, since Claude may use various phrasings.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: model responses with tools
questions.explanation:
'When using tools, Claude often comments on what it's doing or responds naturally to the user before calling tools... This natural response style helps users understand what Claude is doing... It's important to note that Claude may use various phrasings and approaches when explaining its actions. Your code should treat these responses like any other assistant-generated text, and not rely on specific formatting conventions.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** No such marker exists.
- **C.** The text is normal and expected.
- **D.** This is a real and common bug: content[0] may be a text block, so a handler must FIND the tool_use block rather than assume its index. The documented examples all search — 'next(block for block in response.content if block.type == "tool_use")'.

You can 'guide the style and content of these responses through your system prompts and by providing <examples> in your prompts.'
questions.examTrick: Never index content[0] for tool_use — SEARCH the content array by block type. Text often precedes the tool call.

questions.question: Which optional tool-definition property lets a tool's schema be excluded from context until needed?
options: defer_loading
cache_control
allowed_callers
strict
questions.answer: defer_loading
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: tool definition properties
questions.explanation:
The optional properties available on a single tool definition include cache_control, strict, defer_loading, and allowed_callers. defer_loading is the one governing when a schema enters context — the API-side analogue of Claude Code's deferred MCP schemas and tool search.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** cache_control marks the block for prompt caching.
- **C.** allowed_callers restricts which callers may use the tool.
- **D.** strict enables schema validation of the tool's inputs.

A client toolset entry 'accepts cache_control and allowed_callers on the entry and sets defer_loading per member' — so a toolset can defer members individually while caching as a unit.
questions.examTrick: Four optional tool properties: cache_control, strict, defer_loading, allowed_callers. defer_loading is the context-cost lever.

questions.question: A tool named get_data returns a 400-field JSON payload from an upstream API, and the agent frequently picks the wrong field. Which two changes address the root causes?
options: Rename it with a service namespace and a specific verb, expand the description to state exactly what it returns and does not return, and shape the response down to the high-signal fields with semantic identifiers.
Set strict: true and add input_examples.
Force it with tool_choice and increase max_tokens.
Split it into 400 single-field tools so selection is unambiguous.
questions.answer: Rename it with a service namespace and a specific verb, expand the description to state exactly what it returns and does not return, and shape the response down to the high-signal fields with semantic identifiers.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: best practices
questions.explanation:
Two documented problems are present. The generic name and thin description undermine selection: descriptions are 'by far the most important factor', and namespacing 'makes tool selection unambiguous'. The bloated response undermines reasoning: 'Bloated responses waste context and make it harder for Claude to extract what matters.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** strict and input_examples govern INPUTS; the failure here is in naming, description, and OUTPUT shape.
- **C.** Forcing a call does not help the model use the result, and more output tokens do not clarify 400 fields.
- **D.** Directly contradicts the consolidation guidance and would explode both the tool count and the token cost.

The general lesson: diagnose whether the failure is in selection (name/description) or in use (response shape) — they have different fixes.
questions.examTrick: Selection failures → name and description. Use-of-result failures → response shaping. Different problems, different fixes.

questions.question: How are Anthropic-schema client tools such as bash and text editor declared?
options: By a date-versioned type, rather than by writing your own name, description, and input_schema.
By name only, since Anthropic supplies the schema at runtime.
By setting strict: true on an otherwise empty definition.
They cannot be declared explicitly; they are always available.
questions.answer: By a date-versioned type, rather than by writing your own name, description, and input_schema.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: specifying client tools
questions.explanation:
'Anthropic-schema client tools, such as the bash and text editor tools, are declared by a date-versioned type.' The same pattern appears in the server-tool example: {"type": "web_search_20260209", "name": "web_search"}. A user-defined tool instead supplies name, description, and input_schema.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None matches the documented declaration form.

One further distinction: 'The computer use and browser use tools are client toolsets: a single entry with no name that declares a fixed set of member tools.' So there are three shapes — user-defined tools, date-versioned single tools, and toolset entries.
questions.examTrick: Three declaration shapes: user-defined (name+description+input_schema), date-versioned type, and toolset entries with no name.

questions.question: Which is the correct precedence of effort when improving tool reliability, per the documentation?
options: Prioritize descriptions first, then consider input_examples for tools with complex inputs, nested objects, or format-sensitive parameters.
Add input_examples first, then refine descriptions if problems remain.
Set strict: true first, then improve descriptions.
Reduce the number of tools first, then write descriptions.
questions.answer: Prioritize descriptions first, then consider input_examples for tools with complex inputs, nested objects, or format-sensitive parameters.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: best practices
questions.explanation:
'Prioritize descriptions, but consider using input_examples for complex tools. Clear descriptions are most important, but for tools with complex inputs, nested objects, or format-sensitive parameters, you can use the input_examples field to provide schema-validated examples.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Examples cost 20-200 tokens each and are secondary to descriptions.
- **C.** strict addresses conformance, not comprehension — a strictly-validated call to the wrong tool is still wrong.
- **D.** Consolidation is genuinely valuable, but the docs put description quality first as 'by far the most important factor'.

A practical ordering to remember: describe well → consolidate → namespace → shape responses → then add examples and strictness where inputs are genuinely tricky.
questions.examTrick: Descriptions first, always. input_examples are a targeted supplement for complex or format-sensitive inputs.

questions.question: What is the documented naming constraint on a user-defined tool?
options: The name must match the regex ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$.
The name must be lowercase and under 32 characters.
The name must be a valid JavaScript identifier.
There is no constraint on tool names.
questions.answer: The name must match the regex ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools: specifying client tools
questions.explanation:
The parameter table states: 'name: The name of the tool. Must match the regex ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$.' So letters, digits, underscores, and hyphens, between 1 and 64 characters.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Uppercase is permitted and the limit is 64.
- **C.** Hyphens are allowed, which JavaScript identifiers do not permit.
- **D.** There is an explicit regex.

The 64-character budget is what makes service namespacing practical — github_list_pull_request_comments fits comfortably. It also matters when integrating MCP servers, where Claude Code reports and skips a server whose name contains characters outside letters, numbers, hyphens, and underscores.
questions.examTrick: ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$ — letters, digits, underscore, hyphen, up to 64 characters.

questions.question: An agent must never call a destructive tool without prior confirmation from another tool's result. Which design expresses that most reliably?
options: Sequence the workflow so the confirmation tool runs first, disable parallel tool use, and state the prerequisite explicitly in the destructive tool's description — 'only call after X has returned Y'.
Rely on the tool names making the order obvious.
Set strict: true on the destructive tool.
Set tool_choice to any so the model must choose deliberately.
questions.answer: Sequence the workflow so the confirmation tool runs first, disable parallel tool use, and state the prerequisite explicitly in the destructive tool's description — 'only call after X has returned Y'.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools; tool use sequencing
questions.explanation:
Three documented levers combine. The description should explain 'When it should be used (and when it shouldn't)', which is exactly where a prerequisite belongs. disable_parallel_tool_use prevents the model emitting both calls at once. And the exam objective calls for sequencing 'multi-tool workflows so prerequisite data is obtained before dependent tools are called.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Names are weak signals and encode no ordering.
- **C.** strict validates arguments, not call order.
- **D.** any forces SOME call — it could force the destructive one.

Worth adding the enforcement note: if the constraint must hold absolutely rather than reliably, that is a PreToolUse hook's job in Claude Code, or your own execution-layer check in an API application. Descriptions influence; code enforces.
questions.examTrick: Ordering: description prerequisite + disable_parallel_tool_use + turn sequencing. For a hard guarantee, enforce in your execution layer.

questions.question: Which statement about tool descriptions and MCP servers is most accurate?
options: The same description quality principles apply — an MCP server's tool descriptions are what Claude uses to select among them, so vague or overlapping descriptions cause the same wrong-tool failures as with custom API tools.
MCP tool descriptions are ignored because the server name disambiguates.
MCP servers supply their own selection logic, so descriptions do not affect choice.
MCP tool schemas are always loaded in full, so descriptions matter less.
questions.answer: The same description quality principles apply — an MCP server's tool descriptions are what Claude uses to select among them, so vague or overlapping descriptions cause the same wrong-tool failures as with custom API tools.
questions.source: NEW | Claude API docs — Define tools; Claude Code MCP docs
questions.explanation:
Tool selection is driven by descriptions regardless of where the tool comes from. The CCAF objective on improving tool selection reliability names the remedies directly: expanding tool descriptions with use-case examples, input format specifications, and explicit disambiguation guidance for semantically similar tools.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** The server name namespaces the tool but says nothing about when to use it versus a sibling tool on the same server.
- **C.** MCP defines a transport and a tool interface, not a selection policy — selection is the model's, driven by descriptions.
- **D.** The opposite is true in Claude Code: 'full schemas stay deferred and Claude loads specific ones on demand via tool search', so the NAME and DESCRIPTION carry even more of the selection burden.

That last point is the sharp one: under deferred loading, a bad description is all the model has to go on.
questions.examTrick: Under deferred schemas, the description carries the whole selection decision. Vague MCP descriptions fail exactly like vague API ones.
